//: pi config for BOTH review stages (BiggiePockets/.github).
pi resolves models from the config dir pointed at by PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR. This file
declares the OpenRouter provider and every model either stage is allowed to run on,
each with its OpenRouter list rates, so a FRESH CI runner (no cached models-store.json)
resolves them deterministically. These models are absent from the catalog pi ships
and the live catalog refresh is a background fetch, not a startup step we can rely
on.
This is the allowlist behind the workflow's pi_model and codex_model inputs. A repo
may point a stage at any id whose `stages` list names that stage; the workflow fails
early, by name, on a slug that is not listed for the stage requesting it. The default
for Stage 1 is openai/gpt-5.6-luna and for Stage 2 deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash.
`stages` is ours, not pi's. The workflow strips it with jq when it seeds pi's config
dir, so pi only ever sees fields it defines. Keeping it here rather than in a sibling
file means a model and the stages allowed to run it cannot drift apart.
Context: every model here except Claude Haiku 4.5 (200k) carries ~1M tokens. Stage 1
explores the repo over many turns and Stage 2 reads a diff plus the Stage 1 handoff,
so a very large pull request has less headroom on Haiku than the numbers elsewhere in
this file suggest. What a stage actually needs is charted weekly by
scripts/pi/check_model_freshness.py against real usage, not guessed from these specs.
Rates are $/1M tokens exactly as OpenRouter publishes them at the time of pinning.
pi computes cost.total from these. Adding a model means adding its id AND its
published rates together; rolling one means updating both. Note that these are the
model's list rates and routing picks among endpoints that each price it themselves,
so cost.total tracks the bill closely but is not a copy of it.
`routing` is ours, not pi's. The workflow moves it onto every model as pi's
`openRouterRouting` field, which pi sends as-is in the `provider` field of the
OpenRouter request. Declaring it once here rather than per model is deliberate: a
model added without it would quietly route under a different policy than the rest,
and that is not a mistake anything downstream would catch.
The policy is `sort: price` with a throughput floor: among the endpoints serving a
model, prefer the cheapest one that is actually fast enough. Both halves matter.
OpenRouter serves one model from many endpoints at very different prices — as of
pinning, deepseek-v4.1-flash is served by 24, from $0.12/$0.48 up to $0.375/$1.50,
2.5x the rates pinned below. Sorting by throughput alone would hand the route to
whichever of those is fastest at that moment with no ceiling on what it charges, and
since a provider sets its own price and its own serving speed, `fastest` is a lane
anyone can buy. Keeping price as the sort key closes that: an endpoint cannot win by
being expensive. (The `:nitro` slug suffix is the same trap with an extra floor
removed — it is a superset of throughput sorting that also makes priority service
tier endpoints eligible, which are priced above every endpoint in the list above.)
The floor is a preference, not a filter. OpenRouter deprioritizes endpoints that miss
it rather than excluding them, so it can never leave a review with nowhere to run —
unlike `max_price`, which fails the request outright when nothing qualifies. The
worst case here is a slow review, which is what we have today.
p90 30 tok/s is a starting point, not a measurement: it is low enough to shed only
pathologically slow endpoints, so it cannot route worse than the default does. Tune
it against what reviews actually take.
Ids stay plain OpenRouter slugs. check_model_freshness.py looks them up in the live
catalog, and the workflow validates its codex_model/pi_model inputs against them.
The apiKey interpolation reads OPENROUTER_API_KEY from the workflow environment
— no interactive login or OAuth is involved. api/api identify the OpenAI-compatible
endpoint pi uses.
